sourceBindings.text: Bring forward the same three sample IDs, actual start times and final observations from the previous step. After the trainer's selected settling timetable, check that the jar is undisturbed and that the bottom, sand, silt and final mineral boundaries are visible. Exclude floating organic material. Record an unclear interface as unclear rather than copying another jar's line.

Use one ruler and millimetres throughout. A mark measured upward from the bottom is a cumulative height; a layer thickness is the difference between its two bounding marks. If the first mark is 44 mm, the next is 68 mm and the final mark is 80 mm, sand is 44 mm, silt is 68 − 44 = 24 mm and clay is 80 − 68 = 12 mm. The total is 80 mm, not 44 + 68 + 80 mm.

sourceBindings.text: In a well-dispersed classroom jar, the basal mineral layer is generally sand, the middle layer silt and the upper settled mineral layer clay. Read each visible boundary from the bottom upward, and show the three labels beside the matching layers on the diagram.

This jar method offers an approximate picture. Different particle density, incomplete dispersal, irregular jar walls or an unclear boundary can change the apparent layer heights. A USDA class is defined for the fine-earth mineral particle proportions by weight; a height fraction from this classroom jar is not automatically an equivalent laboratory result.

sourceBindings.text: Use the worked 80 mm jar: sand 44 mm, silt 24 mm, clay 12 mm. For each layer, estimated jar percentage = that layer's thickness ÷ 80 mm × 100. This gives 55% sand, 30% silt and 15% clay. Check the raw heights first: 44 + 24 + 12 = 80 mm. Then check 55 + 30 + 15 = 100%.

The total mineral-layer height is always the denominator for this example. If percentages are rounded separately to whole numbers, a sum such as 99% or 101% can be rounding alone; examine unrounded values and stated precision before changing a measurement. A larger mismatch, missing layer or negative difference calls for rechecking marks, subtraction and arithmetic. Record the measured values; do not force a result to 100 by inventing a height.

Then check fifty-five plus thirty plus fifteen equals one hundred percent.

The total mineral-layer height is always the denominator for this example. Record the measured values; do not force a result to one hundred by inventing a height.

sourceBindings.text: First confirm that sand + silt + clay is about 100% with the declared rounding. On the USDA chart used here, find sand 55% on the bottom scale and follow its diagonal line; find clay 15% on the left scale and follow its horizontal line. Verify that the intersecting point also agrees with silt 30% on the right scale. The 55/30/15 point lies in sandy loam, not sandy clay loam. Follow the arrows and printed scales on the actual chart; different graphics can place labels or arrows differently.

The demonstration follows 'I do, we do, you do': watch the 55/30/15 trace, help trace the 30% sand, 30% silt, 40% clay practice point, then trace your own three results. On the standard USDA triangle, the practice point lies on the 40% clay boundary of the clay region; check exact boundary conventions on the chart rather than guessing from the name. A verified USDA calculator can check a completed trace. It does not supply sample data or prove a jar test was done.

sourceBindings.text: The source model table supplies three 100 mm examples: A has 65 mm sand, 25 mm silt and 10 mm clay and is sandy loam; B has 40, 40 and 20 mm and is loam; C has 15, 30 and 55 mm and is clay. These are worked values for learning the method, not observations of your jars. A pre-filled table can help practise division and chart tracing, but it cannot pass the measurement criterion.

For your own A, B and C jars, enter the actual sand, silt, clay and total heights in mm, calculate each percentage, show the intersection on the same chart and state the provisional class. Compare differences between the samples, then carry any water or crop-management interpretation to the next step rather than assuming texture alone decides the whole farm plan.

sourceBindings.text: On the exit card, give one identified sample's three percentages, the traced class and one likely management challenge with the reason. For sandy material, drainage may be faster; for clay-rich material, slow drainage or workability may matter. These are conditional clues, because structure, compaction, organic matter, site and crop also matter. The next step examines such management choices in context.

Keep the distinction explicit: measurements from your own jar, numbers supplied only for practice, and a laboratory texture determination are three different kinds of evidence. If a layer is not measurable, state that limit and ask the trainer whether to observe later or repeat under the declared method.
